module-1: Lankhorst's definition of EA
A coherent whole of principles, methods, and models used in the design and realisation of an enterprise's organisational structure, business processes, information systems, and infrastructure.
Kotusev's definition of EA

A collection of special documents (artifacts) describing an organization from an integrated business and IT perspective, intended to bridge the communication gap between business and IT stakeholders, facilitate IS planning, and improve business and IT alignment.
Bernard's definition of EA
The analysis and documentation of an enterprise in its current and future states from an integrated strategy, business, and technology perspective.
Common standpoint of the EA definitions
Holistic · integrated · business · IS/IT · perspective · principles · practice · documents
Enterprise without EA = ?
A house without blueprints
EA is analogous to…
City planning
Seven additional characteristics of EA

Inherent complexity · Need for structure · Current and future state · Continuously evolves · Requires involvement of whole enterprise · Mutual understanding of diverse perspectives · Communication is key
Why is the architecture process a lifecycle?
Architecture is a process as well as a product: idea → operational system → modify/replace, and it repeats.
Four phases of the architecture process (Lankhorst)
Idea (napkin, whiteboard, PowerPoint) → Design (formal models, analysis) → Use (visualisation for stakeholders, link with implementation) → Management (maintenance, version control)
Six major actors in EA
Business executives · Business unit managers · IT executives · IT project teams · Architects · Third-party (external)
EA is NOT… (8)

One-size-fits-all · Purely technical planning · About the artifacts · Able to transform incompetent decisions/actions · One-time planning · Technology-specific · About implementing frameworks · Enterprise modeling/engineering
Stakeholder
A person or group with an interest (concern) in the enterprise and its architecture; can be individual or aggregated.
Two kinds of EA drivers
Internal drivers (pressures within the organization) and external drivers (pressures outside the organization)
When is good architectural practice indispensable?
Especially when the organization grows and becomes complex.
Organizational alignment
The well-orchestrated interaction of organizational components (hard and soft). Business-IT alignment is especially crucial.
Strategic Alignment Model: who and when?
Henderson and Venkatraman, 1993
Four boxes of the Strategic Alignment Model
Business strategy · IT strategy (external) · Organisational infrastructure and processes · IT infrastructure and processes (internal)
Strategic fit vs. functional integration (SAM)
Strategic fit: external strategy ↔ internal infrastructure (vertical). Functional integration: business ↔ IT (horizontal).
How many dominant alignment perspectives does the SAM give?
Four
Alignment components (Nadler et al., 1992)
Work · People · Formal organization · Informal organization
Organizational alignment (Labovitz & Rosansky, 1997)
Vertical: top strategy ↔ people at the bottom. Horizontal: internal processes ↔ external customers.
EA as management instrument pyramid
Mission → Vision → Strategy → Goals (as-is → to-be) → Actions (EA + culture) → Operations (products, processes, people, IT)
Where does EA sit in the management pyramid?
At the Actions level, with culture (leadership, people).
Why is architecture not a static asset?
It's part of managing the enterprise toward its to-be goals, and those keep changing, so the architecture keeps evolving.
EA role according to Ross et al. (2006)
Successful organizations employ an operating model; EA is the organizing logic for business processes and IT infrastructure, reflecting integration and standardization requirements.
External drivers
Pressures outside the organization; may trigger a push for adoption of an EA practice; external regulations generate substantial impact.
Why is EA unlike building architecture?
Organizations are dynamic socio-technical systems: they can't be engineered then built; they are organic, living entities that evolve over time.
Successful organizations are…
Well-managed evolutions
EA ↔ city planning roles
Business executives ↔ City governors · IT project teams ↔ Construction teams · Architects ↔ City planners
Who are EA architects?
Chief IT planners and owners of EA artifacts; knowledgeable in business and IT with an IT-centric background; effective communicators, team players, innovators.
Five responsibilities of EA architects
Intermediaries between stakeholders · Develop, update, peer-review, approve artifacts · Create and maintain artifact repository · Set up EA software tools · Establish, run, optimize EA processes
What organizations and cities share (any 5)

Can't be perfectly planned · Future needs anticipated, not detailed · Running and evolving at once · Only incremental change · No overnight major change · Poor decisions hinder growth · Endless evolution · No single best way · Multiple concerns
Three major considerations in EA
Communication · Problem of alignment (needs bottom-up process) · Integration of architectural domains
Why is alignment a major challenge?
Each domain is developed by distinct stakeholders with their own concerns and language.
Architectural domains: Kotusev vs. Bernard
Kotusev: various aspects important for business and IT. Bernard: sub-architectures describing distinct functional areas.
Kotusev's six domains
Business · Applications · Data · Integration · Infrastructure · Security
Bernard's five domains
Strategic goals · Workflows · Dataflows · Systems · Infrastructure
Lankhorst's sample domains
Information · Process · Product · Application · Technical architecture
Common language
Crucial. No need to start from scratch; better to use existing elements when possible.
Models as representation
Abstract, unambiguous, formal, many types; capture the essence; only the core of each domain; multiple models usually needed.
Questions when considering a framework
Is it applicable and/or useful to the organization? Is it worth adopting one? If not, what is the alternative?
Bernard's definition: what extra does it capture?
Requirements for the future state (“what does it want to be in the future?”) across short-, medium-, and long-term timelines.
Holistic (common standpoint)
Deals with the entire organization.
Who are business executives vs. business unit managers?
Executives: higher ranks overseeing all departments. Unit managers: department managers, supervisor level.
Examples of IT executives and third parties
IT executives: CTOs, IT/IS department managers. Third parties: consultants, suppliers.
Can the architecture process start anywhere?
Yes. It's not linear; it's an iterative cycle.
Hard vs. soft organizational components
Hard: well documented, formally disseminated, gives structure (job descriptions). Soft: word of mouth, work environment, hard to measure (culture, friendships, attitude).
Pyramid layers in plain words
Mission: why · Vision: where we want to be · Strategy: how to get there · Goals: milestones (as-is → to-be) · Actions: EA gives the roadmap
Process standardization vs. data integration (class)
Standardization: how similar the processes are. Integration: how accessible data is across business units and how well it's used in each department's outputs.
Example of an external driver
Disaster preparedness, like schools during the pandemic; external regulations.
Who decides an organization's domains?
It depends on the organization; you have to talk to them to see their specific domains.
module-2: The four Balanced Scorecard perspectives
Customer · Financial · Internal Business Processes · Learning & Growth
The three layers of each BSC perspective
Mission → Objectives → Measures
Who created the BSC, and what was their point?
Kaplan & Norton (1992): financial measures alone are inadequate. The BSC clarifies vision and strategy.
BSC perspectives where EA is especially useful
Internal Business Processes and Learning & Growth
Business Model Canvas
Osterwalder & Pigneur (2010). A template for a high-level description of new or existing business models. Intuitive layout, used in brainstorming; many elements translate to EA models.
What can serve as a major input to business architecture?
The Business Model Canvas
Business Architecture
A blueprint giving a common understanding of the organization, used to align strategic objectives and tactical demands. A business-oriented abstraction that translates strategy into action.
Capability-based planning
Focus on WHAT (current and desired capabilities) before HOW.
EFQM
European Foundation for Quality Management. Broader than ISO 9001; benchmarks performance against best practices; complements the BSC.
EFQM enablers
Leadership · People · Policy & Strategy · Partnerships & Resources · Processes
EFQM results
People Results · Customer Results · Society Results · Key Performance Results
EFQM criteria where EA is an important instrument
Policy & Strategy and Processes
How EFQM drives continuous learning and innovation
Its principles, measures, and indicators for assessing performance become the basis of continuous learning, innovation, and improvement. The Innovation & Learning loop feeds results back to enablers.
Outlines criteria for a good quality management system (QMS), designed and documented to control how processes are performed. An audit may be requested for certification.
Product realization (ISO 9001)
The business processes that realize the company's product or service.
Key processes under ISO 9001
Those that affect product/service quality.
How EA helps with ISO 9001
Process identification and documentation
COBIT stands for
Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology
COBIT
IT control framework bridging gaps in business risks, control needs, and technical issues. Also gives critical success factors, key goal indicators, and a maturity model for IT governance.
EA vs. COBIT focus
EA: business & IT structures and processes. COBIT: how IT should be organized.
ITIL
IT Infrastructure Library. Widely accepted best practices in IT service delivery. Two process groups: service delivery and service support.
COBIT vs. ITIL
COBIT's control objectives tell WHAT to do; ITIL explains HOW.
Why EA matters to ITIL
EA gives a clear understanding of IT, infrastructure, and business processes, which is crucial to ITIL's management of IT assets.
CMMI
Capability Maturity Model Integration. Assesses the maturity of software engineering processes and gives key practices to increase maturity. Upgraded from SW-CMM in 2000. Five levels.
From which CMMI level is EA especially useful?
Level 3 (Defined) and beyond. EA provides context, constraints, and guidelines for individual software projects.
CMMI vs. COBIT
CMMI: maturity of software engineering (IT implementation). COBIT: IT governance and control.
Outputs of strategic management
Mission · Vision and values · Strategic goals and objectives · Competitive & environmental analysis (e.g., SWOT) · KPIs
Mission vs. vision vs. values
Mission: purpose now. Vision: desired future. Values: guiding principles for behavior.
SWOT
Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats. A competitive and environmental analysis.
The four business strategy problems
1 Generic/vague · 2 No specific IT suggestions · 3 Frequent changes · 4 Short-term systems → alignment trap
Alignment trap
Focusing on new systems for the current strategy. When strategy changes, they become isolated legacy systems that accumulate, turning assets into liabilities.
Middle ground between business and IT
Key discussion points that address concerns on both sides and are understandable and valuable to both.
The five key discussion points
Operating model · Business capabilities · Specific business needs · Business processes · Business requirements
Operating model
Desired organization-wide levels of process standardization and data integration (Ross et al. 2006). Creates four models.
Diversification
Low standardization, low integration. Decentralized; diverse business units. Independence, flexibility, local autonomy.
Replication
High standardization, low integration. Decentralized; similar but independent units. Consistent experience, efficient processes.
Coordination
Low standardization, high integration. Decentralized; diverse interdependent units sharing some data. Superior service, cross- and up-selling.
Unification
High standardization, high integration. Centralized; similar interdependent units. Consistent experience, integrated data, efficient processes.
Why the operating model is a good discussion point
Most abstract and stable; not expected to change in the foreseeable future; very long-term IT planning horizon.
Business capability
General ability to perform a business activity (e.g., customer behavior tracking). Encompasses processes, people, knowledge, and resources. Long-term horizon.
Specific business needs
Addressing a specific business problem using IT (e.g., accurate tracking of work hours). Medium-term (2–3 years).
Business processes
Sequence of activities by specific actors with inputs and outputs. Identifies needed IT systems. Short-term.
Business requirements
Detailed functional and non-functional requirements for a specific system. Most detailed. Actionable in 6–12 months.
Moving up the pyramid
Scope narrows (very wide → very narrow) and planning horizon shortens (very long → very short).
IT initiative
Key unit of work in EA practice resulting in a deployed IT solution or change in the IT landscape, enabling business improvements. Single or multi-project.
Six attributes of an IT initiative
Core business need · Goals and objectives · Scope · Business case (investment, ROI) · Business sponsors · Budget
EA's two questions about IT initiatives
WHAT to implement (optimal portfolio for maximum business value) and HOW (optimal ways to deliver).
Delivery options for an initiative
In-house development · Outsourcing · Off-the-shelf or open source (optionally customized)
Fundamental initiative
Permanent business needs; strategy-agnostic; always necessary. Top-down by C-level and architects, often from the operating model.
Strategic initiative
Stems from current strategy; proposed by top executives for immediate impact. Caveat: may become legacy after the strategy.
Local initiative
Specific local needs; may be unrelated to org strategy. Bottom-up by local executives; reviewed and prioritized by top executives and architects.
Urgent initiative
Urgent needs (overlooked problems, new regulations, new demands). Unplanned; triggered externally; bottom-up; numerous in reality.
Architectural initiative
Improves the overall IT landscape; no direct business need or new functionality. Top-down by architects. E.g., hardware upgrades, decommissioning legacy.
Bottom-up initiative types
Local and Urgent
Why pursue strategic initiatives despite the caveats
Immediate impact on strategy execution and potential competitive advantage; justified when success is likely and the advantage is significant.
COBIT concepts discussed in class
Administration, predictability, information flow (guidance), restrictions, maintenance, rules and regulations, standards, security
CMMI levels 1, 3, and 5
1 Ad hoc: no structure · 3 Defined · 5 Optimized: everything in place and optimized (standard names: 2 Managed, 4 Quantitatively managed)
Capability examples from class
“Buy and sell products online”; “Ateneo can handle classes online”
Alignment trap in plain terms
Hiring people and creating departments only for one goal or system; when the strategy is scrapped, they're no longer used.
Diversification in one line (class)
Acquiring businesses unrelated to the core business.
Why is Disney Coordination?
Low standardization (hotels, theme parks, film studio) but high integration (shared branding and customer experience).
When do fundamental initiatives change?
Only if the organization changes industry; otherwise they stay the same whatever the operating model.
How are strategic initiatives judged?
Risk assessment with probabilities: high risk, high reward; if it works, it gives competitive advantage.
module-3: Four phases that need support in the architecture life cycle
Design · Communication · Realization · Change
Support in the design aspect (3)
Common, well-defined vocabulary · Organization-wide guidelines, best practices, standards · Tracking architectural changes and decisions
Why a common vocabulary?
It doesn't focus on a single domain; it allows integration of architectures from different domains.
Support in the communication aspect
Share with stakeholders within and outside the organization; visualize relevant aspects per stakeholder group; emphasize relations (connections and dependencies) among domains.
Support in the realization aspect
Design considerations on a more detailed level; integration between different design tools.
Support in the change aspect
A change in one architecture may affect others in different domains; assess the consequences.
Compositionality
The standard way of dealing with complexity: distinguish the parts of a system and the relations between them (e.g., parts of a car working together).
Integration of architectural domains
One way to deal with EA complexity; gives insight. Some problems can't be solved, and they can't be eliminated; concepts and tools only make them easier to deal with.
Integration problem #1
Different modeling standards/languages (UML, BPMN) per domain; one-to-one mapping of elements across domains is hard. E.g., entities/relations vs. classes/objects.
Integration problem #2
Integrating structural and behavioral models. E.g., software components vs. application functions; ERD vs. DFD.
Structural vs. behavioral models (class)
Structural: static parts and how it's built. Behavioral: processes and how it operates over time. Faucet analogy: parts vs. water flow.
Domain
An area of knowledge, influence, or ownership. Framework-dependent.
Traditional vs. modern domains
Modern example: cloud
Where could you start when choosing domains?
Business and IT, then possibly break down further.
Questions to ask when deciding on domains (5)
Major stakeholders and their focus · Priority areas · Capabilities, strengths, weaknesses · Is the approach flexible enough? · How easy to integrate chosen domains?
What is of more value to EA than full detail?
The essence of each domain, with focus on relations and interactions between domains.
Model (definition)
An abstract and unambiguous conception of something in the real world, using a formalized graphical or textual language.
What does a model's rigor require?
Architects must be more meticulous.
Universe-enterprise analogy
Enterprise = universe; stakeholder = viewer; the viewer's conception = architecture; its representation = architecture description (models, text).
Architecture vs. architecture description
Architecture: the stakeholder's conception. Architecture description: its representation in models and textual descriptions.
What shapes a stakeholder's conception?
Interests (concerns); individual or aggregated level; preconceptions: social, cultural, educational, professional background.
Domain (3.2 meaning)
A subset of the conception of the universe
Modeling
The act of abstracting a model from a part of the universe, using some language and medium.
View vs. viewpoint
View: what one sees. Viewpoint: where one is looking from. A view is specified through a viewpoint.
Who is interested in the full scope of the architecture?
Only architects. Other stakeholders need specific views.
Single model for the whole enterprise?
Ideal but infeasible. In practice, partial models from different domains make a collective whole.
Content vs. visualization
Content: concepts involved. Visualization: how content is presented. Architecture should be independent of visualization.
Pictures and diagrams vs. models
Pictures and diagrams should not be equated with models.
Architecture semantics
Inherent meaning. Two distinct views of the same thing have common elements; consistency is advantageous.
Symbolic model
Represents architecture properties using symbols that refer to reality, with formal syntax and notation called a description language. UML focuses on this.
Semantic model
Represents one possible interpretation of a symbolic model. ArchiMate emphasizes this.
What does the common vocabulary build on?
Everyday language colleagues use, plus technical terms known in the organization or key domains.
What can happen when changes aren't assessed?
They can snowball across domains.
Compositionality in EA terms
Break the enterprise down into manageable parts: the architectural domains.
How do structural and behavioral models affect each other?
Both ways: water pressure can break the faucet; the faucet's structure affects the output pressure.
Why keep the number of symbols low?
So stakeholders aren't overwhelmed and can understand the model.
Architectural conception vs. architecture description
Conception: intangible, undocumented understanding of each stakeholder group. Description: tangible representation in artifacts (models, text).
Picture vs. model: interpretations
A picture can have multiple interpretations; a model has only one.
Which matters more in EA: symbolic or semantic?
Semantic. Symbolic models can be too technical for other stakeholders.

items.q: A bank's IT team launched a mobile app, but marketing says it doesn't support their campaign goals at all. Which internal driver is this mostly about?
items.w: Internal driver: organizational alignment, and business-IT alignment is especially crucial (1.2 slide 5).

items.q: The central bank issues a rule that all banks must report transactions digitally. A bank starts an EA practice to cope. This pressure is:
items.w: External drivers come from outside the organization; regulations generate substantial impact and may trigger adoption of an EA practice (1.2 slide 11).

items.q: A company's job descriptions are clear, but employees follow “how things are really done here” instead. The mismatch is between:
items.w: Hard = documented and formal (job descriptions); soft = word of mouth, culture, attitude (class).

items.q: The CEO and the frontline staff describe the company's goals completely differently. Which alignment is weak?
items.w: Vertical alignment links top strategy with people at the bottom (Labovitz & Rosansky, 1.2 slide 8).

items.q: A hospital's internal processes don't match what its patients actually need. Which alignment is weak?
items.w: Horizontal alignment links internal processes with external customers (1.2 slide 8).

items.q: The IT strategy calls for moving to cloud services, but the current IT infrastructure can't support it. In the SAM, which link is broken?
items.w: Strategic fit is the vertical link between external strategy and internal infrastructure (1.2 slide 6).

items.q: The business strategy targets online sales growth, but the IT strategy focuses only on cutting hardware costs. In the SAM, which link is weak?
items.w: Functional integration is the horizontal link between the business side and the IT side (1.2 slide 6).

items.q: An architect sketches an idea for a new student portal on a whiteboard during a meeting. Which phase of the architecture process is this?

items.q: The architect presents tailored diagrams of the portal to the registrar and to students. Which phase?
items.w: Use: visualisation for different stakeholders, link with implementation (1.1 slide 12).

items.q: After launch, the architect maintains the models and keeps version control as the portal changes. Which phase?
items.w: Management: maintenance and version control (1.1 slide 12).

CMMI enables the assessment of the maturity of <u>IT governance</u> processes.
The strategic management process produces a <u>low-level</u> business strategy that defines long-term direction.
Business strategy often requires <u>reusable</u> IT components.
When business strategy gives little guidance, IT planners are often forced to decide based on <u>guesswork</u>.
Competitive advantage and market segmentation are examples of <u>purely business</u> concerns.
The operating model was discussed in the 2006 paper by <u>Kaplan and Norton</u>.
<u>Unification</u> is the only centralized operating model.
The Diversification model offers independence, flexibility, and local <u>autonomy</u>.
In the Replication model, business units are similar and <u>interdependent</u>.
Specific business needs are a <u>convenient</u> discussion point for business and IT.
Business processes approximate how solutions should work and which <u>activities</u> need to be changed.
The operating model has the <u>narrowest</u> planning scope among the discussion points.
Strategic initiatives may be proposed directly by <u>local executives</u> for immediate impact on strategy execution.
Approved <u>urgent</u> initiatives are prioritized after review by top executives and architects.

The Business Model Canvas is <u>rarely</u> used during brainstorming sessions.
Business architecture is a <u>technology</u>-oriented abstraction that helps translate strategy into action.
EFQM <u>complements</u> the Balanced Scorecard.

COBIT provides a maturity model for IT governance, similar to <u>ITIL</u>.

CMMI was upgraded in 2000 from <u>COBIT</u>, with an expanded scope.
<u>KPI analysis</u> is an example of a competitive and environmental analysis.
“Increase market share by 15% in three years” is <u>specific enough</u> to guide IT planning.
Current IT systems are assets, but they may become <u>liabilities</u> under the next strategy.
The middle ground between business and IT should be valuable in the short, long, and <u>very long</u> term.
Relational databases are an example of a <u>purely business</u> concern that is meaningless to IT stakeholders.
The operating model shapes the overall reporting structure and defines the level of <u>autonomy</u>.
In the Unification model, business units are similar and <u>independent</u>.
Superior customer service, cross-selling, and up-selling are benefits of the <u>Replication</u> model.
Business capabilities change in a major way only when the core <u>business model</u> shifts.
Moving up the pyramid of discussion points, the planning scope becomes <u>wider</u>.

In communication, it is very important to emphasize <u>relations</u> among different domains.
For better realization, design considerations must go on a <u>less</u> detailed level.
A change in one architecture <u>never</u> affects others in different domains.

<u>All</u> integration problems can be solved.

M1.q: A bank's IT team launched a mobile app, but marketing says it doesn't support their campaign goals at all. Which internal driver is this mostly about?
M1.w: Internal driver: organizational alignment, and business-IT alignment is especially crucial (1.2 slide 5).

M1.q: The central bank issues a rule that all banks must report transactions digitally. A bank starts an EA practice to cope. This pressure is:
M1.w: External drivers come from outside the organization; regulations generate substantial impact and may trigger adoption of an EA practice (1.2 slide 11).

M1.q: A company's job descriptions are clear, but employees follow “how things are really done here” instead. The mismatch is between:
M1.w: Hard = documented and formal (job descriptions); soft = word of mouth, culture, attitude (class).

M1.q: The CEO and the frontline staff describe the company's goals completely differently. Which alignment is weak?
M1.w: Vertical alignment links top strategy with people at the bottom (Labovitz & Rosansky, 1.2 slide 8).

M1.q: A hospital's internal processes don't match what its patients actually need. Which alignment is weak?
M1.w: Horizontal alignment links internal processes with external customers (1.2 slide 8).

M1.q: The IT strategy calls for moving to cloud services, but the current IT infrastructure can't support it. In the SAM, which link is broken?
M1.w: Strategic fit is the vertical link between external strategy and internal infrastructure (1.2 slide 6).

M1.q: The business strategy targets online sales growth, but the IT strategy focuses only on cutting hardware costs. In the SAM, which link is weak?
M1.w: Functional integration is the horizontal link between the business side and the IT side (1.2 slide 6).

M1.q: An architect sketches an idea for a new student portal on a whiteboard during a meeting. Which phase of the architecture process is this?
The architect turns the sketch into formal models and analyzes them. Which phase?
M1.w: Design: formal models and analysis (1.1 slide 12).

M1.q: The architect presents tailored diagrams of the portal to the registrar and to students. Which phase?
M1.w: Use: visualisation for different stakeholders, link with implementation (1.1 slide 12).

M1.q: After launch, the architect maintains the models and keeps version control as the portal changes. Which phase?
M1.w: Management: maintenance and version control (1.1 slide 12).

M1.q: A consultant says: “Just adopt this famous framework and your EA problems are solved.” Based on the slides, what's wrong with this?
o: EA is not about implementing frameworks
M1.a: EA is not about implementing frameworks
M1.w: “About implementing frameworks” is on the EA is NOT list (1.1 slide 14).

M1.q: A company wants to redesign every department at once, overnight. Why won't this work, using the city-planning view?
o: Organizations change through incremental modifications, not overnight
Organizations can be perfectly planned in every detail
There is one best way to evolve
M1.a: Organizations change through incremental modifications, not overnight
M1.w: Organizations and cities can't be changed entirely; major changes don't happen overnight (1.3 slide 9).

M1.q: A university finished its EA documents in 2020 and hasn't updated them since. What's the problem?
o: EA continuously evolves; it isn't one-time planning
Nothing; EA is finished once documented
M1.a: EA continuously evolves; it isn't one-time planning
M1.w: EA continuously evolves and is not one-time planning; architecture is not a static asset (1.1, 1.2).

M1.q: Each department in a company models its own area in its own terms, and the models don't line up. Which major consideration from 1.3 is this?
o: The problem of alignment across domains
M1.a: The problem of alignment across domains
M1.w: Alignment is a major challenge because each domain is developed by distinct stakeholders with their own concerns and language (1.3 slide 11).

M2.q: A school's retention target is 70%, but the best schools reach 85%. Which standard helps raise the target?
M2.w: EFQM benchmarks organizational performance against best practices (2.1 slide 11; class example).

M2.q: A manufacturer wants a certificate showing its quality management system passed an audit.
M2.w: Once a QMS is installed, an audit may be requested for certification (2.1 slide 13).

M2.q: The CIO wants control objectives that link business risks, control needs, and technical issues.
M2.w: COBIT is an IT control framework bridging gaps in business risks, control needs, and technical issues (2.1 slide 14).

M2.q: Help desk tickets keep closing late; management wants best practices for service delivery and support.
M2.w: ITIL: widely accepted best practices in IT service delivery; groups are service delivery and service support (2.1 slide 15).

M2.q: A company is choosing between two outsourcing vendors and compares how mature their software development processes are.
M2.w: CMMI assesses the maturity of software engineering processes (2.1 slide 16).

M2.q: Management tracks graduation rate, cost per degree, teaching effectiveness, and faculty development side by side.
M2.w: These are measures across the four BSC perspectives (2.1 slide 7).

M2.q: In a brainstorming workshop, a startup puts its customers, channels, and revenue streams on one page.
M2.w: The canvas gives a high-level description of a business model and is often used in brainstorming (2.1 slide 8).

M2.q: Before choosing any system, a university decides it needs “the ability to run classes online.” This is:
M2.w: Business architecture uses capability-based planning: focus on what (capabilities) before how (2.1 slide 10).

M2.q: Different managers read “We will be the best telco in Asia” in completely different ways.
o: Business strategy problem #1: generic, open to interpretation
M2.a: Business strategy problem #1: generic, open to interpretation
M2.w: Problem #1: generic statements subject to different interpretations (2.2 slide 8).

M2.q: The strategy lists revenue targets but says nothing about which systems to build, so IT guesses.
o: Business strategy problem #2: no specific IT suggestions
M2.a: Business strategy problem #2: no specific IT suggestions
M2.w: Problem #2: no practical IT suggestions; IT planners decide by guesswork (2.2 slide 9).

M2.q: Leadership changes direction every six months, and half-finished IT projects keep getting abandoned.
M2.w: Problem #3: frequent changes give no solid basis for IT planning and wreak havoc on IT plans (2.2 slide 10).

M2.q: A company built a custom system and hired a team just for a promo strategy. When the strategy ended, both sat unused.
M2.w: Focusing on new systems for the current strategy can lead to the alignment trap: assets become liabilities (2.2 slide 11; class).

M2.q: Every branch of a coffee chain follows the same recipes and service steps, but each branch keeps its own sales records.
M2.w: High process standardization, low data integration; similar but independent units (2.2 slide 15).

M2.q: A bank's savings, credit card, and insurance units run differently but share one customer record to cross-sell.
M2.w: Low standardization, high integration; diverse interdependent units sharing data; cross- and up-selling (2.2 slide 15).

M2.q: HR says: “We need to reduce payroll errors from manual time logs using IT.” Which discussion point is this?
M2.w: A specific business problem addressed using IT; medium-term (2.2 slide 18).

M2.q: The board launches a 3-year plan to enter e-wallets and orders a wallet app. If the plan is dropped, the app loses its purpose.
M2.w: Stems from the current business strategy; danger of becoming legacy after it (2.3 slide 10).

M3.q: Architects agree on one shared vocabulary so the process team and the application team can relate their models.
M3.w: Design support: a common, well-defined vocabulary that allows integration across domains (3.1 slide 5).

M3.q: An architect logs every major architectural decision so the team can backtrack when something breaks.
M3.w: Design support includes tracking architectural changes and decisions (3.1 slide 5).

M3.q: The architect shows the finance team only the parts relevant to them and leaves out technical detail.
M3.w: Communication: visualize relevant aspects for a particular stakeholder group (3.1 slide 6); class: filter information.

M3.q: The architect adds more detail so developers can implement the design, and connects the different modeling tools the teams use.
M3.w: Realization: more detailed design considerations; integration between design tools (3.1 slide 7).

M3.q: Switching the database vendor broke three business processes nobody had checked.
o: Change: consequences across domains weren't assessed
M3.a: Change: consequences across domains weren't assessed
M3.w: A change in one architecture may affect others; assess the consequences (3.1 slide 8). Class: it can snowball.

M3.q: The process team models in BPMN and the application team in UML; nobody can map a process step to an application component.
M3.w: Different standards per domain make one-to-one mapping of elements hard (3.1 slide 11).

M3.q: The team has an ERD of the data and a DFD of the processes but can't explain how they relate.
M3.w: ERD (structural) vs. DFD (behavioral): how are they related? (3.1 slide 13).

M3.q: To understand a complex hospital, the architect lists its parts (departments, systems) and how they connect to each other.
M3.w: Compositionality distinguishes the parts of a system and the relations between them (3.1 slide 9).

M3.q: A nurse and the CFO describe the same hospital very differently because of their roles and backgrounds.
o: Stakeholder concerns and preconceptions shape their conception
M3.a: Stakeholder concerns and preconceptions shape their conception
M3.w: Interests and social, cultural, educational, professional background shape each conception (3.2 slide 7).

M3.q: The dean sees enrollment numbers and budgets but not the IT network design.
o: A view from the dean's viewpoint
M3.a: A view from the dean's viewpoint
M3.w: Viewpoint = where one looks from; view = what one sees; visible elements depend on the stakeholder (3.2 slide 9).

M3.q: Students share an undocumented sense of “what Ateneo is.” The architect captures it in models and text. The models and text are the:
M3.w: The conception is the architecture; its representation in models and text is the architecture description (3.2 slide 6).

M3.q: An architect draws an attractive picture of the system, but each manager reads it differently.
o: Pictures aren't models; a model has one interpretation
M3.a: Pictures aren't models; a model has one interpretation
M3.w: Pictures and diagrams should not be equated with models (3.2 slide 11); class: pictures allow multiple interpretations.

M3.q: The same org chart is drawn once as a pyramid and once as boxes and lines, and it means the same thing.
o: Architecture should be independent of visualization
M3.a: Architecture should be independent of visualization

M3.q: Business managers find the UML diagrams too technical, so the architect presents a version focused on what the elements mean.
M3.w: Symbolic models can be too technical; semantic models are easier for stakeholders and matter more in EA (3.2 slide 12; class).

M3.q: Management asks for one diagram that shows the entire enterprise for everyone. Why is this a problem?
o: A single model is ideal but infeasible; partial models form the whole
Single models are illegal under COBIT
M3.a: A single model is ideal but infeasible; partial models form the whole
M3.w: Single model for the enterprise is ideal but infeasible; partial models from different domains make a collective whole (3.2 slide 10).
